cues.text: Let us work through some additional diagnostic and optimisation examples.
These show how the ideas of loss, delay, throughput and traffic control come together when you have to measure a network, explain a complaint, or answer an exam question.
We begin with a measurement example.
Suppose you send 1,000 probes and receive 980 replies.
That means 20 probes got no reply.
Twenty out of 1,000 is 2 percent, so the loss is 2 percent.
Now look at delay.
Suppose the round-trip times, or RTTs, are 20, 22, 70 and 23 milliseconds.
To find the mean RTT, add the four values: 20 plus 22 is 42, plus 70 is 112, plus 23 is 135.
Divide 135 by 4 and you get 33.75 milliseconds.
Notice that the 70 millisecond sample is far above the others.
That sample is a delay spike.
The mean of 33.75 milliseconds hides it, because the average sits well above the typical samples and well below the spike.
This leads to a careful point about jitter.
You should specify how jitter is measured, rather than treating mean delay as jitter.
Mean delay tells you the average level of delay.
Jitter is about variation, so whichever way you measure it, state the method.
The last point in this example links loss to throughput.
TCP retransmissions can lower goodput, which is the useful data actually delivered, because retransmitted data uses sending effort without adding new data.
Congestion control also adjusts the sending rate.
So loss can cause reduced throughput even on a high-capacity link.
A link with plenty of capacity does not guarantee high throughput if loss is making TCP slow down.
Now a practical case.
An ISP customer reports slow evening service.
How do you investigate?
Collect several kinds of evidence.
First, interface utilisation and errors.
Second, access-link signal or optical metrics.
Third, flow volumes.
Fourth, RTT and throughput to several controlled endpoints.
Using several endpoints matters, because it lets you compare different parts of the path.
Then compare peak and off-peak data.
If the problem appears in the evening but not at quieter times, that pattern is itself evidence.
Next, segment the path.
By measuring along different sections, you can distinguish between three possibilities: last-mile congestion, a transit problem, or a remote-service problem.
The same thinking applies in a university.
Separate critical exam traffic from bulk updates.
Schedule large transfers off peak.
Correct faulty links.
Upgrade sustained bottlenecks, meaning places where congestion persists rather than appearing briefly.
Then verify application completion rates, to confirm that the changes helped the applications people actually depend on.
One qualification must be remembered: prioritisation does not guarantee capacity outside managed domains.
You can prioritise traffic within networks you manage, but that does not create capacity beyond them.
Finally, here is an exam answer on traffic shaping versus policing.
Shaping queues excess traffic and sends it later.
This reduces burstiness, at the cost of delay.
Policing, by contrast, drops or remarks excess traffic immediately.
So the trade-off is this: shaping smooths traffic by waiting, while policing acts at once by dropping or remarking.
When should you use each?
Use shaping toward a known slower uplink, and use policing to enforce a contract at ingress, as appropriate.
Also, bound voice priority to prevent starvation.
If voice has strict priority without a limit, it could consume so much of the service that other traffic is starved.
Putting a bound on voice priority prevents that.
